title: Good zeal (Rule 72)
hookLine: outdo one another in honor; prefer nothing to Christ
tomorrow: Francis's well-known song: what happens if you read it to the end?

cards: Some comment sections have one person who cares enormously, is completely sure, and is making everyone around them miserable. The caring isn't the problem. Benedict knows it.

In chapter seventy-two of his Rule he says there are two kinds of zeal. A bitter zeal, which separates people from God. And a good zeal, which separates people from their vices and leads to God and to everlasting life.
Same heat, two directions. The bitter kind can be very busy, and very sure of itself. So what does the good kind look like?

teach.b: Benedict's answer is a short list, and every line points at other people. Practice it with the warmest love, he says, and he borrows Paul's words to the Romans: "in honour preferring one another."
Try to outdo each other in honor. Bear one another's weaknesses, of body or of character, with great patience. Nobody chasing what seems good for himself, but what's good for someone else.
Compete in obeying one another. Love one another with a pure, brotherly love.

Then the line that holds it together: prefer nothing whatever to Christ, and may he bring us all together to everlasting life. Together. Good zeal is a race where the aim is to let someone else go first.
A neighbor tradition says something close.
In Pirkei Avot, the Mishnah's collection of the sayings of the sages, Rabbi Eliezer teaches: let your friend's honor be as dear to you as your own.

Two traditions, each lifting another person's honor up to where we usually keep our own. The difference is honest too. Benedict's reason is Christ, preferred above everything, the center of his whole Rule.
The sages of the Mishnah speak from a life of Torah, and Christ isn't part of their teaching.
A shared instinct, rooted in different ground. Here's the one to tell a friend: Benedict's cure for zeal gone bitter isn't less fire.
It's fire pointed at someone else's good.

how: Monks and nuns who follow the Rule of Benedict hear chapter seventy-two as part of the Rule read aloud in community.

o: a warm eagerness that puts other people's honor first
a drive to fast and pray longer than the others
being fierce and loud in arguing for your faith

p: leads to God and to life
a friend's honor, dear as your own

s: Benedict says all zeal is dangerous, so monks should avoid it
the skimmer's reading. he names a bitter zeal and a good zeal, and asks for the good one with the warmest love.
Benedict borrows Paul's line about preferring one another in honor
it comes from Paul's letter to the Romans.
Benedict pictures the best monks reaching everlasting life on their own
he prays that Christ will bring us all together.

games.q: two volunteers at the food drive start competing over who sorted more boxes, and it's getting tense. what does good zeal do?
o: keep score; a little rivalry gets more boxes sorted.
care less; the zeal itself is the problem here.
race to give the other one the credit first.
games.why: Benedict keeps the fire and turns it around: outdo one another in honor. the contest becomes who can honor the other first.

practice: Count on your fingers the people whose work helped you this week without much thanks: someone who covered for you, cooked, drove, explained. For each finger, picture one way to give them the credit first.
Let the sit end on the last face.

wordCard.voice: Good zeal. In Benedict's Rule, the warm fire that leads to God by putting other people's honor first.

orig.note: Benedict's Latin word for zeal: a burning eagerness that can turn bitter or good.

carryVoice: Keep this: prefer nothing to Christ, the line Benedict says holds the rest together. Day sixteen-thirty, done.
